title: AC circuits
examples: What is the difference between AC and DC circuits?
How does reactance affect the current in a circuit?
Can you explain what phasors help us visualize?

explain.say: Today we explore alternating current circuits in detail. We will look at three key concepts. These are root mean square, reactance, and phasors.

The root mean square value gives an effective measure of AC current. It tells us the equivalent DC value for power calculations. For a sine wave, the rms value is the peak voltage divided by the square root of two.
Reactance is the opposition to current flow in AC circuits. It is caused by inductors and capacitors. Inductive reactance increases with the frequency of the alternating current.

Capacitive reactance decreases as the frequency increases. This is because capacitors store and release charge quickly. The formula for capacitive reactance involves dividing one by the frequency times the capacitance.

Phasors are a way to represent sinusoidal voltages and currents using vectors. They allow us to show the phase difference between voltage and current. The phase angle tells us how much they are out of sync.
In a real-life example, household AC power uses rms values. Your wall socket voltage is rated in rms volts. This value is used to calculate the actual power delivered to your appliances safely.

faq.q: What is the difference between peak voltage and rms voltage?
faq.a: Peak voltage is the maximum voltage reached by the wave. The rms voltage is the effective value that represents the power delivered, which is lower than the peak value.
asks: How do I find the effective voltage?
What does 'rms' stand for in voltage?

faq.q: Does reactance only happen in inductors?
faq.a: No, reactance also occurs in capacitors. Inductors create inductive reactance, and capacitors create capacitive reactance.
asks: What causes opposition in AC circuits?

faq.q: What does the phase angle tell us?
faq.a: The phase angle tells us the time difference between the voltage and the current. This difference is crucial for calculating the power in the circuit.
asks: Why do I need to know the phase difference?
What is the relationship between voltage and current phases?

faq.q: Are phasors just another way to draw waves?
faq.a: Phasors are a mathematical tool that simplifies the analysis. They represent the sinusoidal function using a rotating vector, making calculations easier.
asks: How are phasors better than drawing waves?

faq.q: If frequency increases, what happens to capacitive reactance?
faq.a: If the frequency increases, the capacitive reactance decreases. This means the capacitor offers less opposition to the current flow.
asks: What happens to capacitors at high frequencies?

facts: The rms value relates to the square root of the average of the square of the values.
Inductive reactance ($XL$) increases linearly with frequency ($f$).
Capacitive reactance ($XC$) is inversely proportional to frequency ($f$).
Phasors use the cosine function to represent sinusoidal quantities.

quiz.say: If a voltage has a peak value of 10 volts, what is its rms value?
quiz.why: The rms value is correctly calculated by dividing the peak voltage by the square root of two.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the peak voltage by the square root of two.
wrong.1: This assumes the peak value is the same as the rms value, which is incorrect for AC.
wrong.3: This confuses the calculation with simple division instead of using the square root.

quiz.say: What happens to inductive reactance when the frequency doubles?
quiz.why: Since inductive reactance is directly proportional to frequency, doubling the frequency doubles the reactance.

wrong.0: This ignores the direct mathematical relationship between $XL$ and $f$.
wrong.1: This incorrectly uses a squared relationship instead of a linear one.
wrong.3: This incorrectly suggests an inverse relationship between frequency and inductive reactance.

quiz.say: If the current leads the voltage by a phase angle $\phi$, what is the circuit component likely to be?
quiz.why: In a capacitive circuit, the current waveform reaches its peak before the voltage waveform, causing the current to lead the voltage.

wrong.0: This is too general; the specific relationship (leading/lagging) points to capacitance.
wrong.2: In an inductive circuit, the voltage leads the current, not the other way around.
wrong.3: In a purely resistive circuit, the current and voltage are in phase, meaning there is no leading or lagging.
